level.vistulans_880.title: Prince of the Vistulans
level.vistulans_880.goal: Methodius warns a pagan prince on the Vistula. The prince laughs, and the prophecy comes true: he will be baptised as a captive
level.vistulans_880.hint: The advice was given, but history did not follow it. A prince baptised of his own free will would never have been taken captive, and we need things as they were.
level.vistulans_880.intro: Around 880. On the upper Vistula, where Kraków will one day stand, a mighty pagan prince rules the Vistulans. To the south Great Moravia of Prince Svatopluk is growing, and there the Slavic teacher Methodius is preaching: the man who, with his brother Cyril, gave the Slavs their alphabet.
level.vistulans_880.fact: The Life of Methodius tells how a pagan prince “on the Vistula” mistreated Christians, and Methodius sent word to him: “It would be good for you, my son, to be baptised of your own will on your own land, lest you be baptised by force as a captive in a foreign land; and then you will remember me.” The prince did not listen. Soon Svatopluk of Moravia conquered the Vistulans, and, the Life says, the prince was indeed baptised in captivity. This is the first mention in written sources of the lands of future Lesser Poland, almost a century before the baptism of Mieszko.
level.chrobry_crown_1025.title: The First King
level.chrobry_crown_1025.goal: Bolesław the Brave waits twenty-five years for a crown, and puts it on the moment the emperor dies
level.chrobry_crown_1025.hint: Asking the emperor is pointless: he will say “no”, and it will be remembered. Sometimes the best move is to wait.
level.chrobry_crown_1025.intro: 1024. Bolesław the Brave is the strongest ruler between the Elbe and the Dnieper: he fought Emperor Henry II for fifteen years and never lost. A royal crown was promised to him back in 1000 at Gniezno, but Henry will never allow it. Bolesław is nearly sixty.
level.chrobry_crown_1025.fact: On 13 July 1024 Henry II died without a son, and the empire began electing a new king. While the Germans had no time for Poland, at Easter 1025 the archbishop in Gniezno crowned Bolesław, the first King of Poland. He reigned as king for only two months and died on 17 June 1025. A German chronicler wrote with irritation that Bolesław had “usurped” the crown; he was succeeded by his son Mieszko II, crowned that same year.
level.chrobry_crown_1025.source: Annals of Quedlinburg; Gallus Anonymus, Deeds of the Princes of the Poles
level.magdeburg_1257.title: Kraków Under Magdeburg Law
level.magdeburg_1257.goal: After the Mongol fire, Kraków is rebuilt from scratch under German law, with self-government and a vast Market Square
level.magdeburg_1257.hint: A town is people, but not just any people: the duke has his own peasants and had no intention of giving them up. You lay out a square once there are people to trade in it.
level.magdeburg_1257.intro: 1257. Sixteen years ago the Mongols burned Kraków to the ground. Duke Bolesław the Chaste wants the capital of Lesser Poland to rise again quickly and richly, and he summons three wójts to build the city on the model of German towns.
level.magdeburg_1257.fact: On 5 June 1257 Bolesław the Chaste granted the wójts Gedko, Jakub and Dytmar a charter: Kraków received Magdeburg law, with its own court, a town council and liberties for the burghers. In the middle of the city a Market Square was laid out, about 200 by 200 metres and one of the largest medieval squares in Europe, surrounded by a grid of straight streets that survives to this day. The charter had a crafty clause: the wójts were forbidden to admit the duke's peasants to the city, because the duke did not want to lose his subjects or their taxes. From there Magdeburg law spread across Poland: by the 16th century hundreds of towns lived under it.
level.kalisz_1264.title: The Statute of Kalisz
level.kalisz_1264.goal: The Duke of Greater Poland places the Jews under the protection of the law, and for centuries Poland becomes home to the largest Jewish community in the world
level.kalisz_1264.hint: A community rests on the law, not the other way round. Slander builds nothing; it only destroys.
level.kalisz_1264.intro: 1264. Terrible libels against the Jews are spreading across Europe, and they are expelled from one town after another. The Duke of Greater Poland, Bolesław the Pious, does the opposite and invites them into his towns: he needs trade, money and crafts.
level.kalisz_1264.fact: On 16 August 1264 in Kalisz, Bolesław the Pious issued a statute: a Jew was to be judged by the duke, not by the mob; killing a Jew meant death and confiscation; no one could accuse Jews of using Christian blood, and a Christian who made such a charge and failed to prove it suffered the same penalty. The statute even had a touching clause: if a Jew cried for help at night and his Christian neighbours did not come, they paid a fine. Casimir the Great extended the statute to the whole kingdom, and over several centuries hundreds of thousands of Jews settled in Poland. In 1580 the communities even received their own “parliament”, the Council of Four Lands.
level.kalisz_1264.source: Statute of Kalisz of Bolesław the Pious, 1264
level.academy_1400.title: The Queen's Jewels
level.academy_1400.goal: The dying Jadwiga leaves her jewels to the university, and Jagiełło revives the Kraków Academy
level.academy_1400.hint: The king has only one treasury, and the temptation to spend it on war with the Order is great. Without the will there is nothing to open.
level.academy_1400.intro: 1399. The university founded by Casimir the Great has almost faded away since his death. Queen Jadwiga dreams of reviving it, but she is gravely ill after childbirth. War with the Teutonic Order draws ever closer, and the lords count every coin.
level.academy_1400.fact: Jadwiga died on 17 July 1399 and bequeathed her jewels to the revival of the academy. On 26 July 1400 Jagiełło reopened it in a house bought from the Pęcherz family of burghers, today the Collegium Maius; its first rector was Stanislaus of Skarbimierz, and the first speech was a sermon on the value of learning. A hundred years later Nicolaus Copernicus would study here. Today it is the Jagiellonian University, one of the oldest in Europe.
level.academy_1400.source: Jan Długosz, Annals, under 1399–1400; Jagiełło's charter of 26 July 1400
level.nihil_novi_1505.title: Nihil novi
level.nihil_novi_1505.goal: The Sejm at Radom decides that the king can introduce nothing new without the nobility's consent, and noble democracy is born
level.nihil_novi_1505.hint: The lords will offer the king an easy path: rule by the few. The nobility's voice must first be chosen back home in the province.
level.nihil_novi_1505.intro: 1505. King Alexander Jagiellon is squeezed between powerful magnates and a numerous nobility. Four years ago the magnates wrung the Privilege of Mielnik from him: all power to the Senate. Now the nobility, about a tenth of the population, demands its share.
level.nihil_novi_1505.fact: On 30 May 1505 the Sejm at Radom passed the constitution “Nihil novi nisi commune consensu”, “nothing new without common consent”: the king could not make laws without the Senate and the Chamber of Deputies. The Privilege of Mielnik never came into force. In 1506 Chancellor Jan Łaski published the first printed code of Polish law, Łaski's Statute, with an engraving of the king in the Sejm. Noble democracy was unique in Europe: a tenth of the country could vote, many times more than in France or England at the time. Its shadow was the peasantry, which had no vote at all.
level.rej_1562.title: Poles Are Not Geese
level.rej_1562.goal: Mikołaj Rej, a nobleman with poor Latin, starts writing in Polish and becomes “the father of Polish literature”
level.rej_1562.hint: Learned advice is not always useful: Latin will lead the book away from its reader. The nobleman will be the one reading, so write for him.
level.rej_1562.intro: The 16th century. Educated Poland speaks and writes in Latin: laws, science, theology and poetry are all in Latin. Mikołaj Rej of Nagłowice is a self-taught nobleman who never properly learned Latin. But he knows how people talk at the market, in the tavern and on the manor.
level.rej_1562.fact: Rej wrote only in Polish: satires, sermons, moral tales, The Life of an Honest Man. In 1562, in his collection The Menagerie, he left a line every Polish schoolchild knows: “let the neighbouring nations know that Poles are not geese, they have a tongue of their own” (the honking of geese being a jibe at Latin). Alongside him worked Jan Kochanowski, the first great poet of the Polish language: in 1580 he published the Laments, a lament for his two-year-old daughter Urszula, and for the first time in Poland private grief became high poetry.
level.rej_1562.source: Mikołaj Rej, The Menagerie (1562); Jan Kochanowski, Laments (1580)
level.grain_gdansk.title: The Granary of Europe
level.grain_gdansk.goal: Polish rye floats down the Vistula to Gdańsk and on to Amsterdam: the nobility's wealth rests on the serf
level.grain_gdansk.hint: Grain does not grow by itself: first someone has to work the lord's field. If the peasant runs away, there will be nothing to sell.
level.grain_gdansk.intro: The 16th century. The Netherlands and Western Europe are growing and need bread. Poland has black soil and the Vistula, which flows straight to Gdańsk. The nobleman realises it pays better not to collect rent from his peasants but to sow for the market himself, with those same peasants' hands.
level.grain_gdansk.fact: In 1496 the Sejm forbade peasants to leave their villages freely, and the Statute of Toruń of 1520 imposed compulsory labour service, one day a week; by the 17th century it reached three to six days. The lords' folwark estates sent rye down the Vistula on rafts and szkuta barges; the raftsmen, the flisaks, were called “Vistula sailors”. Gdańsk became the largest port on the Baltic, and the Dutch called the Baltic grain trade “the mother of all trades”. The nobility grew rich and built palaces, while peasants fled the labour service to the borderlands and the Dnieper steppes.
level.grain_gdansk.source: Statute of Toruń (1520); M. Małowist, East and West Europe in the 13th–16th Centuries
level.batory_1579.title: King of Men, Not of Consciences
level.batory_1579.goal: Stephen Báthory gives the Jesuits a university in Vilnius, yet lets no one be persecuted for their faith
level.batory_1579.hint: The king must first become king, and the condition of the election is known. A zealous preacher is dangerous to someone nobody protected.
level.batory_1579.intro: 1576. After Henry of Valois flees, the nobility elects the Transylvanian prince Stephen Báthory, on condition that he marry Anna Jagiellon, sister of the last Jagiellon. He is a Catholic who favours the Jesuits, and the Jesuit Piotr Skarga is the finest preacher in the land. But all around are Calvinists, Lutherans and Orthodox, and everyone remembers the oath of the Warsaw Confederation.
level.batory_1579.fact: On 1 May 1576 Báthory married Anna and was crowned on the same day. He supported the Jesuits: on 1 April 1579 he raised their college in Vilnius to an academy, the first university of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania, with Piotr Skarga as its first rector. Yet he firmly kept the peace between faiths. He is credited with the words: “I am king of men, not of consciences.” The Calvinist Mikołaj Radziwiłł the Red remained his hetman and chancellor of Lithuania. The Vilnius Academy is today Vilnius University.
level.batory_1579.source: Stephen Báthory's privilege for the Vilnius Academy (1579); R. Heidenstein, Commentaries on the Muscovite War
level.arians_1658.title: The Expulsion of the Polish Brethren
level.arians_1658.goal: A country that swore not to persecute for faith expels the Arians, and their books, printed in Amsterdam, change the thinking of Europe
level.arians_1658.hint: You can stay only by renouncing your faith, and then there will be no book. They will print where no one is persecuted for their faith.
level.arians_1658.intro: 1658. Poland has barely survived the Swedish “Deluge”. People look for someone to blame and find them: the Polish Brethren, or Arians, Protestants who rejected the Trinity. Their academy at Raków was closed twenty years ago, and now the Sejm decides their fate. Among them is the philosopher Andrzej Wiszowaty, grandson of the movement's founder Faustus Socinus.
level.arians_1658.fact: The Sejm of 1658 ordered the Arians to convert to Catholicism within three years or leave the country; later the deadline was cut to two. Around 1660 several thousand people left for Transylvania, Prussia and the Netherlands. Wiszowaty settled in Amsterdam and in 1665–1668 published the Bibliotheca Fratrum Polonorum, a multi-volume collection of the Polish Brethren's writings. Their ideas on freedom of conscience and reason in faith were read by John Locke, Pierre Bayle, Voltaire and Newton. And so the country that in 1573 had sworn never to shed blood over faith expelled an entire confession for the first time.
level.arians_1658.source: Constitution of the Sejm of 1658 “On the Arians”; Bibliotheca Fratrum Polonorum (Amsterdam, 1665–1668)
level.ken_1773.title: The First Ministry of Education
level.ken_1773.goal: During the First Partition, Poland creates the Commission of National Education, the first ministry of education in Europe
level.ken_1773.hint: There is money for schools, as long as it isn't pilfered on the way. Whoever is loudest about “distributing” it is the most dangerous of all.
level.ken_1773.intro: 1773. Poland has just lost a third of its lands in the First Partition; the Sejm sits under the eye of the Russian ambassador, and the Sejm's marshal, Adam Poniński, is a paid agent of the neighbours. Then news arrives from Rome: the pope has dissolved the Jesuit order, which ran almost every school in the country.
level.ken_1773.fact: On 14 October 1773 the Sejm established the Commission of National Education, the first state education authority in Europe. It was given the Jesuits' property, and former Jesuits often stayed on as teachers. The Commission published new textbooks in Polish, introduced physics, natural science and even hygiene, and in 1777–1780 Hugo Kołłątaj reformed the Kraków Academy. To be honest, Poniński's Distribution Commission did embezzle a good part of the Jesuit riches, but what remained was enough for the schools to outlive the Partitions themselves.
level.ken_1773.source: Constitution of the Sejm of 14 October 1773; T. Mizia, On the Commission of National Education
level.mickiewicz_1834.title: Pan Tadeusz
level.mickiewicz_1834.goal: After the uprising is crushed, Mickiewicz writes Pan Tadeusz in Paris, a book that became a home for Poles
level.mickiewicz_1834.hint: To believe in forgiveness is to risk everything. The poem is written in exile, and its listeners are those who left with the poet.
level.mickiewicz_1834.intro: 1832. The November Uprising has been crushed. Some ten thousand insurgents, officers, poets and musicians leave through Germany for France; it will be called the Great Emigration. The emperor promises an amnesty to those who return. Among those who left is Adam Mickiewicz, already the most famous poet in Poland.
level.mickiewicz_1834.fact: Many who trusted the amnesty were arrested and exiled. Mickiewicz stayed in Paris and in 1834 published Pan Tadeusz, an epic of a noble manor in Lithuania in 1811–1812, of quarrels, hunts, love and hope in Napoleon. The poem opens with the line “Lithuania, my country, thou art like health”, which Poles know by heart. Paris in those years also held Chopin, Słowacki and Lelewel: the country was gone from the map, but its culture lived on in exile. In 2012 the whole country read Pan Tadeusz aloud in the first National Reading.
level.lodz_1880.title: The Promised Land
level.lodz_1880.goal: A village grows into Łódź, the “Polish Manchester”, where factory owners build palaces and weavers stand at the looms for twelve hours
level.lodz_1880.hint: Cloth needs a buyer, and the biggest buyer lies beyond the eastern customs line. There won't be enough hands if the workers walk out.
level.lodz_1880.intro: The second half of the 19th century. Poland is gone from the map, but chimneys smoke in the Kingdom of Poland. Not long ago Łódź was a village; now Poles, Jews and Germans are flocking here to build factories and work in them. Izrael Poznański started with a shop and is now building a textile empire.
level.lodz_1880.fact: In 1851 the customs border between the Kingdom of Poland and Russia was abolished, and the empire's huge market opened to Polish cloth. After the abolition of serfdom in 1864, peasants poured into Łódź. The city grew faster than any other in Europe: from a few hundred inhabitants in 1820 to about 300,000 by 1900. Poznański built factories, workers' housing and a palace nicknamed “the Louvre of Łódź”. In 1892 the workers of Łódź staged one of the first mass strikes in the empire. Władysław Reymont described the city in his novel The Promised Land, and in 1924 he won the Nobel Prize.
level.flying_university_1885.title: The Flying University
level.flying_university_1885.goal: Women in Warsaw are forbidden to study, so a secret university wanders from flat to flat, and young Maria Skłodowska studies there
level.flying_university_1885.hint: The secret is kept not by a lock but by movement: the courses won't last in one place. Maria will get to Paris in time; first, here.
level.flying_university_1885.intro: 1885. Warsaw, in the Russian Empire. The university teaches only in Russian and does not admit women at all. A teacher, Jadwiga Dawidowa, decides: if it can't be done openly, we will teach in secret.
level.flying_university_1885.fact: From 1885 Dawidowa organised underground courses that became known as the Flying University: classes were held in private flats, in a new place each time, to evade the police. The best Warsaw professors taught history, chemistry, physics and philosophy, in Polish. Thousands of women passed through the courses, among them Maria Skłodowska, who left for Paris in 1891 and later became the first woman to win a Nobel Prize, and twice at that. In 1906 the university came out of hiding as the Society of Scientific Courses.
